106.title: The eleven blessings
106.hook: sleep well, wake well, no bad dreams, dear to people and to other beings
106.howItsDone: Some Buddhists practice or chant metta before sleep, and the eleven benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya are recited in teachings and on protective chanting occasions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karaniya: the metta sutta, and a mother protecting her only child. Your line was as a mother. Did someone get that look from you, for a breath? Day one hundred and six.

It's midnight. You're in bed, and your mind is replaying an argument from this afternoon. What you said. What you should have said. What you'll say next time. Your heart is going a little fast. Sleep is not coming. The clock says twelve-forty, then one-fifteen. Today's text makes a promise that sounds surprisingly modern. It's a short list from the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of numbered teachings, and the very first thing on it is this: a person who practices loving-kindness sleeps well.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, REPLAYING THE ARGUMENT.` → `SLEEP ISN'T COMING.` → `THE FIRST BLESSING: SLEEP WELL.`

segments.voice: The text is called the Metta Sutta too, a different one, in the Book of Elevens. The Buddha lists eleven benefits for someone who practices metta often and well. Let's go through them. One, you sleep well. Two, you wake well. Three, you don't have bad dreams. Four, you're dear to people. Five, you're dear to non-human beings, which the tradition understands as spirits and other unseen beings. Six, the gods protect you. Seven, fire, poison and weapons don't harm you. Eight, your mind settles quickly into concentration. Nine, your face is bright and clear. Ten, you die without confusion. And eleven, if you go no further on the path, you're reborn in a heavenly realm, the Brahma world. Now, how do people hear a list like that? Different Buddhists hear it in different ways. Some take all eleven at face value, including protection from fire and weapons, and chant metta for protection. Others hear the first few especially as plain observations. It isn't hard to see why a mind that isn't nursing grudges would sleep better, or why people warm to someone who warms to them. The text itself doesn't explain; it lists. But notice where it starts: not with enlightenment, not with the heavens. With sleep. The practice begins in the most ordinary place in your life. And that closes ten days of metta: four phrases, yourself, a benefactor, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, the barriers broken, all beings, the sutta, and now its blessings. Tomorrow the path turns to the breath.
screen: `THE BOOK OF ELEVENS.` · `SLEEP WELL, WAKE WELL, NO BAD DREAMS.` · `DEAR TO PEOPLE AND UNSEEN BEINGS.` · `IT BEGINS WITH SLEEP.` · then, large: `KINDNESS SLEEPS WELL.`

segments.voice: This practice is made for bedtime, but you can try it now. Sit or lie down, and let the body get heavy. Let the breath slow. Bring to mind anyone from today, the pleasant and the difficult, one at a time, and offer each a single wish: may you be at ease. Don't linger. Let each one go, like closing doors softly down a hallway. Finish with yourself: may I be at ease. Tonight, try it again as you fall asleep. The bell holds the time.
Anguttara Nikaya. The collection of numbered teachings where the Buddha lists eleven blessings for loving-kindness, starting with sleeping well.
Your line: kindness sleeps well. Tonight, before sleep, send one wish to everyone you met today, and one to yourself. Day one hundred and six.

some take all eleven at face value; others hear some as plain observations.

what it means: eleven benefits of metta practiced often, from sleep to a peaceful death.

107.title: Sixteen steps
107.hook: the breathing discourse gives sixteen steps in four groups of four
107.howItsDone: Anapanasati is taught in Theravada monasteries and in meditation centers in many countries, and practice begins with simply knowing the in-breath and the out-breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anguttara Nikaya's eleven blessings, starting with sleep. Your line was kindness sleeps well. How did you sleep? Day one hundred and seven, and ten days with the breath begin.

Since you woke up this morning, you've breathed thousands of times, and you didn't have to think about a single one. Breathing happens whether you pay attention or not. And it only ever happens now. You can't take yesterday's breath, or tomorrow's. Maybe that's why the Pali texts give it a discourse of its own. It's number 118 in the Middle Length Discourses, the Anapanasati Sutta. And it takes something you do without thinking, and turns it into a whole path, in sixteen steps.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF BREATHS SINCE MORNING.` → `ONLY EVER NOW.` → `A WHOLE PATH IN SIXTEEN STEPS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is anapanasati. The standard explanation splits it in three. Ana: breathing in. Apana: breathing out. Sati: mindfulness. Mindfulness of breathing in and out. The discourse opens on a full-moon night at the end of the rainy season. Many monks are gathered, and the Buddha is so pleased with them that he stays another month. Then he teaches this. It begins simply. A person goes to a forest, or the foot of a tree, or an empty room. Sits down, legs crossed, body upright, and sets mindfulness in front. Mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. Then come the sixteen steps, in four groups of four. The first four are about the body: the long breath, the short breath, the whole body, calming the body. The second four are about feeling: joy, ease, noticing feelings, calming them. The third four are about the mind: knowing it, gladdening it, steadying it, freeing it. And the last four are about seeing clearly: change, fading, ending, letting go. Body, feeling, mind, and the way things are. That's a map of the whole inner life, and every step of it rides on one breath. The discourse makes a big claim: this simple practice, developed and made much of, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, and those lead on to awakening. Over the next ten days, you'll walk these steps a few at a time. They aren't meant to be finished in a week. But every step begins exactly where you already are: breathing in, breathing out. Sixteen steps, one breath.
screen: `ANA, APANA, SATI.` · `SIT, SET MINDFULNESS IN FRONT.` · `BODY, FEELING, MIND, SEEING.` · `EVERY STEP RIDES ON ONE BREATH.` · then, large: `SIXTEEN STEPS, ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit the way the discourse describes, as best you can: upright, but not stiff. Chair or cushion is fine. Let your attention rest at the front of the body, where the breath is easiest to feel: the nostrils, the upper lip, or the chest. Don't change the breath. Just know it. Breathing in, you know you're breathing in. Breathing out, you know you're breathing out. When the mind wanders, and it will, just come back to the next breath. If you'd like, try five minutes later today. The bell holds the time.
Anapanasati. Mindfulness of breathing in and out, taught in sixteen steps.
Your line: sixteen steps, one breath. Today, three times, stop and know one whole breath, in and out. Day one hundred and seven.

108.title: Long and short
108.hook: steps one and two: a long breath known as long, a short breath as short
108.howItsDone: Buddhist breath meditation usually begins with simply knowing the breath as long or short, as the discourse describes, without controlling it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anapanasati: mindfulness of breathing, in sixteen steps. Your line was sixteen steps, one breath. Did you catch three whole breaths? Day one hundred and eight, and step one.

Most breathing advice you'll find tells you to do something. Breathe in for four, hold for seven. Belly breathing. Box breathing. Deep breaths before the presentation. Those have their uses. But the first step of the Buddhist breathing discourse is stranger, and harder, than any of them. It doesn't ask you to change anything. Not the length, not the rhythm, not the depth. It asks you to notice. That's all. And anyone who has tried it for sixty seconds knows how hard that is.
screen: `IN FOR FOUR, HOLD FOR SEVEN.` → `CHANGE NOTHING.` → `JUST NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Here are steps one and two, from the Middle Length Discourses. Breathing in long, a person knows: I breathe in long. Breathing out long, they know: I breathe out long. Breathing in short, they know: I breathe in short. Breathing out short, they know: I breathe out short. That's it. No instruction to make the breath long. The breath is whatever it is. Your job is to know it. There's a lovely picture for this in the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. A skilled wood turner at his lathe, pulling the cord. When he makes a long pull, he knows he's making a long pull. When he makes a short pull, he knows it's short. No fuss. The knowing sits right alongside the doing. Why start here? Because the moment you try to watch the breath, you'll notice something funny: you start controlling it. The breath gets stiff and self-conscious, like someone who knows they're being photographed. Step one is learning to watch without grabbing. Let the breath breathe itself, and let the knowing come along for the ride. And the words long and short are useful because they're simple. Not good or bad, not deep enough, not right. Just long, or short. Relaxed breathing tends to be longer; tense breathing, shorter. You'll start to notice which one you're in, which tells you how you actually are, before your mind has come up with a story about it. That knowing, without judging and without fixing, is the root of everything that follows. Just know it.
screen: `BREATHING IN LONG, KNOW IT'S LONG.` · `THE WOOD TURNER'S LONG PULL.` · `WATCH WITHOUT GRABBING.` · `NOT GOOD OR BAD: LONG OR SHORT.` · then, large: `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath do whatever it does. On each in-breath, silently notice: long, or short. On each out-breath: long, or short. Don't try to make it long. If you catch yourself controlling it, that's fine. Let go, and wait for the next breath to arrive on its own. If you can't tell whether it's long or short, just know: breathing in, breathing out. Later today, you might give this five minutes. The bell holds the time.
Long and short. Steps one and two of the breathing discourse: knowing the breath as it is, without changing it.
Your line: just know it. Today, in one tense moment, check: is my breath long or short? Just know it. Day one hundred and eight.

109.title: The whole body
109.hook: steps three and four: sensing the whole body, calming it
109.howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation, practitioners move from simply knowing the breath to feeling it through its whole length, or through the whole body, and letting the body grow calm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, long and short: steps one and two, knowing the breath as it is. Your line was just know it. In a tense moment, was your breath long or short? Day one hundred and nine.

Right now, without moving, notice your shoulders. Are they up near your ears? Now your jaw. Is it clenched? Your forehead. Your hands. Is any of them holding on for no reason at all? It's easy to carry a body around all day like a bag you've forgotten you're holding. Steps three and four of the breathing discourse bring the body back into the picture. First, feel all of it. Then, let it settle.
screen: `SHOULDERS UP NEAR YOUR EARS?` → `A BAG YOU FORGOT YOU'RE HOLDING.` → `FEEL ALL OF IT. LET IT SETTLE.`

segments.voice: Notice a small shift in the words here. Steps one and two said: a person knows. Steps three and four say: a person trains. They train like this: experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in; experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out. Then: calming the body's activity, I will breathe in; calming it, I will breathe out. Knowing has become training. Something is being gently developed now. But what does the whole body mean? Here's where Buddhists read the text differently, and it's worth knowing both. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, says the body here is the body of the breath: you feel each breath from its beginning, through its middle, to its end, the whole length of it, not just the tip. Some modern teachers read it as the physical body: you let the breath be felt everywhere, chest, belly, back, shoulders, the whole body breathing. Both readings are practiced today, and the text itself doesn't settle it. And then step four: calming. The word for the body's activity, in a related discourse, is explained as the breath itself. So as you feel the whole body, the breath naturally softens and slows, and the body goes quiet with it. You don't force it. You create the conditions, and the settling happens, like mud sinking to the bottom of a still glass of water. The shoulders come down. The jaw lets go. The body settles.
screen: `FROM KNOWING TO TRAINING.` · `THE WHOLE BREATH, OR THE WHOLE BODY?` · `CALMING THE BODY'S ACTIVITY.` · `MUD SINKING IN STILL WATER.` · then, large: `THE BODY SETTLES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find the breath. Now widen your attention, so you feel each breath from its very beginning to its very end. Then widen further: feel the breath moving the belly, the chest, the back, the shoulders. The whole body breathing. As you breathe out, let one place soften: the jaw, then the shoulders, then the hands. Don't force the calm. Just let the body find its own stillness, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
Kaya. Body: steps three and four of the breathing discourse, feeling the whole breath, or the whole body, and letting it calm.
Your line: the body settles. Today, three times, feel one whole breath through your body, and let your shoulders drop. Day one hundred and nine.

110.title: Joy and ease
110.hook: steps five and six: breathing with gladness, breathing with ease
110.howItsDone: Following these steps, Buddhist meditation teachers encourage students to notice and allow the joy (piti) and ease (sukha) that arise as the mind settles, rather than treating practice as grim effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaya, the whole body: steps three and four, feeling it all and letting it calm. Your line was the body settles. Did your shoulders drop today? Day one hundred and ten.

Meditation has a reputation for being a bit like flossing. Good for you, mildly unpleasant, something to get through. So it's a surprise when the Buddhist breathing discourse, at step five, says: breathe with joy. And at step six: breathe with ease. Not grim endurance. Gladness. And there's a story behind that, one you already know from camp two. A young man, starving himself in the forest, suddenly remembers a happy afternoon from long ago, and asks himself a question that changes everything.
screen: `MEDITATION AS FLOSSING?` → `BREATHE WITH JOY.` → `A QUESTION THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Remember the rose-apple tree. In a discourse called the Mahasaccaka Sutta, after he has pushed his body through harsh practice to the edge of death, the Buddha-to-be recalls a day long before, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father was busy, and slipping into a quiet, happy stillness. And he asks himself: why am I afraid of that pleasure? It has nothing to do with craving or harm. That question turned him toward the middle way. Steps five and six carry the same insight. The person trains: experiencing joy, I will breathe in and out. Experiencing ease, I will breathe in and out. Today's word is piti, joy or rapture: the bright, lifting, sometimes tingling gladness that can arise when the mind settles. Its partner is sukha, a softer happiness, ease, contentment. The old manual, the Visuddhimagga, tells them apart with a picture. A traveler lost in the desert, exhausted, sees a pool of water up ahead: that's piti, the thrill. Then he reaches it, drinks, and bathes: that's sukha, the deep ease. Both are welcome. Both are part of the path. Now, you don't manufacture these feelings. When the body settles, as it did in steps three and four, pleasure tends to show up on its own: warmth, lightness, a quiet smile. The practice is simply to let it in, instead of brushing it off as a distraction. That can be the hard part, if you've learned to trust only effort and discomfort. The discourse trains the other way. You're allowed to enjoy it.
screen: `WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT PLEASURE?` · `PITI: JOY. SUKHA: EASE.` · `THE POOL SEEN, THE POOL REACHED.` · `LET IT IN.` · then, large: `YOU'RE ALLOWED TO ENJOY IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the body settle, the way you did yesterday. Now look for anything pleasant, however small: the warmth of your hands, the softness of the out-breath, the quiet in the room, the relief of sitting down. Don't create anything. Just find what's already there. When you notice something pleasant, let it be felt, fully, for a breath or two. If nothing seems pleasant, notice what's neutral and easy; that counts too. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Piti. Joy, gladness, the bright lift that can come when the mind settles. Step five of the breath.
Your line: you're allowed to enjoy it. Today, when something is pleasant, a meal, the sun, a laugh, stay with it for one extra breath. Day one hundred and ten.

111.title: Feeling the mind
111.hook: steps seven and eight: knowing the mind's activity and calming it
111.howItsDone: In breath meditation, Buddhists learn to notice the feeling tone of each moment and the mind's labels, letting the mind's activity calm by knowing it clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, piti: joy, and its quieter partner, ease. Your line was you're allowed to enjoy it. What did you stay with for one extra breath? Day one hundred and eleven.

You wake up and something feels off. Nothing has happened yet. No bad email, no argument. But there's a gray cloud sitting over the morning, and by nine o'clock you've decided the day is bad, your job is bad, maybe your life is a bit bad. Then someone makes you laugh at lunch, and the cloud's gone, and you can't remember what it was. Moods are like weather. They blow in and blow out. Steps seven and eight of the breathing discourse teach you to watch the weather, and let it calm.
screen: `A GRAY CLOUD OVER THE MORNING.` → `GONE BY LUNCH.` → `MOODS ARE LIKE WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Steps seven and eight close the second group of four, the group about feeling. The person trains: experiencing the mind's activity, I will breathe in and out. Calming the mind's activity, I will breathe in and out. What's the mind's activity? A related discourse, the Culavedalla Sutta, gives an answer: feeling and perception. Feeling here doesn't mean emotion exactly. It's vedana: the basic tone of every moment, pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Perception is how the mind labels things: that's a threat, that's a friend, that's boring. Together they're the machinery underneath a mood. Something feels slightly unpleasant, the mind labels it, and before you know it, there's a story and a storm. Step seven is watching that machinery run, with the breath as your anchor. Oh, there's unpleasant. There's the label. There's the cloud forming. You're not the weather; you're the one watching the sky. And step eight, calming, follows the same pattern as step four did for the body. You don't argue with the mood or wrestle it down. Knowing it clearly, breath after breath, lets it soften by itself. A storm you're watching is a very different thing from a storm you're lost in. This is also where the discourse starts moving inward. The first four steps were about the body. These four have been about feeling. Next come four about the mind itself. It's a map that starts in the most physical place, the breath in your nose, and walks you gently inside. Calm the weather.
screen: `THE MIND'S ACTIVITY: FEELING AND LABEL.` · `PLEASANT, UNPLEASANT, NEITHER.` · `YOU'RE THE ONE WATCHING THE SKY.` · `KNOWN CLEARLY, IT SOFTENS.` · then, large: `CALM THE WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle with the breath for a few moments. Now ask gently: what's the weather in here? Sunny, cloudy, stormy, foggy? Don't fix it. Just name it. Then notice its tone: is this moment pleasant, unpleasant, or neither? Keep breathing. If a mood is strong, feel where it sits in the body, and let each out-breath be a little softer than the last. You're not chasing the cloud away. You're watching it move. The bell holds the time.
Vedana. Feeling, the basic tone of pleasant, unpleasant or neither: steps seven and eight, knowing the mind's activity, and letting it calm.
Your line: calm the weather. Today, when a mood rolls in, say to yourself: weather. Then take one slow breath. Day one hundred and eleven.

112.title: Gladdening the mind
112.hook: steps nine to twelve: the mind known, gladdened, steadied, set free
112.howItsDone: In breath meditation, Buddhist practitioners learn to recognize the mind's state and respond to it: brightening a heavy mind, gathering a scattered one, and loosening whatever it's gripping.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vedana, feeling the mind: moods as weather, known and calmed. Your line was calm the weather. Did you catch a mood rolling in? Day one hundred and twelve, and the end of the week.

A kid on a bike, training wheels just off, wobbling down the sidewalk. A good parent doesn't yell. They don't grab the handlebars either. They jog alongside, say something encouraging, steady the seat for a second, and then, at the right moment, let go. That's almost exactly the shape of the next four steps in the breathing discourse. They're about the mind itself: getting to know it, cheering it up, steadying it, and finally, letting it go free.
screen: `A KID LEARNING TO RIDE.` → `ENCOURAGE, STEADY, LET GO.` → `FOUR STEPS FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The third group of four in the breathing discourse is about citta, the mind or heart. Step nine: experiencing the mind, I will breathe in and out. Just knowing what state the mind is in right now. Busy or quiet, dull or bright, tight or open. Step ten: gladdening the mind. If the mind is heavy or discouraged, you gently lift it. The old manual connects this with the gladness that comes as the mind settles; some teachers also suggest remembering something good, a kindness, a moment of calm, the qualities of the Buddha. Not fake cheer: just enough encouragement to keep going. Step eleven: steadying the mind, concentrating it. If it's scattered, you bring it together, collecting it on the breath the way you'd gather loose papers into a neat stack. And step twelve: liberating the mind. The old manual explains this as freeing the mind from whatever is binding it in that moment: dullness, restlessness, grasping at a thought. Loosening the knot, one breath at a time. So there's a real skill in these steps. You're learning to read your own mind, the way a good gardener reads the soil, and give it what it needs. If it's sluggish, brighten it. If it's scattered, gather it. If it's caught, let it go. That's not suppressing anything. It's care. And look back at this week: eleven blessings of kindness, then the breath in sixteen steps. Long and short. The whole body. Joy and ease. The weather of the mind. And now, the mind gladdened and released. Twelve of the sixteen steps. Tomorrow, the last four.

segments.voice: Sit, and settle with the breath. Now ask: what's my mind like right now? Just notice. If it feels heavy, bring to mind one good thing from today, and let it brighten you a little. If it feels scattered, count a few breaths to gather it. If it's gripping a thought, feel the grip, and on the out-breath, loosen it, like opening a fist. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Citta. Mind, heart: steps nine to twelve of the breathing discourse, known, gladdened, steadied, and set free.
Your line: release. Today, when you notice your mind clenched around something, take one breath and loosen the grip. Day one hundred and twelve.
